chapters: Elephants: memory, matriarchs and the meaning of death

units.t: Amazing Animals. Episode one.
In this episode: How clever are animals, Ants: the superorganism, Elephants: memory, matriarchs and the meaning of death and Senses beyond our own.
Part one. How clever are animals.
Crows that craft tools, dolphins with names, elephants that cooperate.
Animal minds are far richer than we once assumed, and harder to measure.
Measuring minds.
Comparing intelligence across species is hard.
Each animal evolved to solve its own world's problems: a squirrel remembers thousands of buried nuts, a bat navigates by echoes, a bee learns which flowers pay off.
Tests designed around human strengths can make other species look dull.
Gibbons were once thought slow because they failed a classic test: using a stick to rake in a banana.
The researcher Benjamin Beck realised their hook-like hands, built for swinging through trees, were poor at that kind of handling.
When he redesigned the test to suit their bodies, the gibbons did well.
Researchers also follow Morgan's Canon, set out by the British psychologist C. Lloyd Morgan in 1894: don't credit an animal with a higher mental ability if a simpler one explains the behaviour.
Tool makers.
New Caledonian crows make tools in the wild, shaping hooked sticks and cutting stepped strips from pandanus leaves to extract grubs.
In a famous 2002 Oxford experiment, a crow named Betty bent a straight wire into a hook to lift a food basket from a tube.
Crows also drop stones into water to reach floating food.
American researchers who wore a mask while trapping crows found the birds scolded that mask for years, and taught other crows to do the same.
In 1960, Jane Goodall saw chimpanzees at Gombe strip leaves from twigs to fish termites from mounds, a shock when tool-making was seen as uniquely human.
Chimpanzee communities have different traditions, which young animals learn over years, and orangutans and bonobos also use tools.
Whether apes can learn human language is debated.
Culture and cooperation.
In Shark Bay, Western Australia, some bottlenose dolphins tear off marine sponges and wear them over their beaks while probing the seafloor for fish, protecting themselves from scrapes.
Mothers pass 'sponging' mainly to their calves, especially daughters, which makes it a form of culture.
Each dolphin also develops a signature whistle.
Others copy it to call that individual, and the dolphin responds, so the whistles work much like names.
Elephant families are led by an older female, the matriarch, whose knowledge of water, dangers and routes can be vital in droughts.
In Kenya, families with older matriarchs were better at telling familiar from unfamiliar calls and at reacting to male lion roars.
In experiments, pairs of elephants learned to pull two ends of a rope together, and waited for a partner before pulling.
The mirror test.
In 1970, psychologist Gordon Gallup Jr developed the mirror test.
An animal gets time with a mirror, then a coloured mark is placed where it can only see it in the reflection.
If it uses the reflection to touch or inspect the mark, it may recognise the image as itself.
Great apes passed, along with some bottlenose dolphins, an Asian elephant and Eurasian magpies.
Humans usually pass at around 18 months to two years.
But the test relies on vision, so it may be unfair to animals that experience the world through smell or sound.
Dogs usually fail, yet a 2017 study found they spent longer sniffing their own urine when its scent was altered.
Some gorillas may avoid eye contact.
In 2019 a cleaner wrasse apparently passed, sparking debate about what the test measures.
What this means.
Complex minds have evolved many times, in very different bodies.
Birds' brains are wired differently from ours but can pack in large numbers of neurons, and octopuses, bees, parrots, rats and pigs all show impressive learning.
In 2012, a group of scientists signed the Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, stating that many animals possess the brain systems that support conscious experience.
You can see animal smarts yourself: watch local magpies, crows or cockatoos solve problems, or try puzzle feeders with a dog.
Recognising animal minds has practical weight too, informing debates about farming, zoos, research and wildlife protection.
The key idea: Intelligence is hard to compare across species, so tests need careful controls and fair design.
Part two. Ants: the superorganism.
There may be around 20 quadrillion ants on Earth.
Individually simple, together they farm, build, wage war and solve problems no single ant could.
A planet of ants.
Sit on almost any patch of Australian ground for a few minutes and an ant will find you.
In 2022, researchers combined hundreds of studies and estimated about 20 quadrillion ants on Earth, roughly two and a half million per person.
Together, they estimated, ants weigh more than all wild birds and wild mammals combined.
More than 14,000 species have been named, and many more await description.
Australia is especially rich, with well over a thousand known species.
Ants live almost everywhere except the coldest places, from rainforest canopies to the hottest deserts, and they shape their environments by moving soil, spreading seeds and eating other insects.
One colony, one animal.
A typical colony is a family.
At its heart are one or more queens, whose job is laying eggs.
Almost all the ants you see are workers, which are female and usually do not reproduce.
Males appear only to mate, and die soon after.
Workers divide the jobs of caring for young, building and defending the nest, and foraging.
Biologists call the colony a superorganism, with workers a little like cells in a body.
No ant is in charge.
They communicate mainly with pheromones.
A forager that finds food lays a scent trail home.
Shorter routes are reinforced faster, because round trips are quicker, so the colony settles on efficient paths without a plan.
This emergent behaviour has inspired 'ant colony optimisation' in computing.
Farmers and herders.
Humans began farming roughly 12,000 years ago, but some ants have been doing it for tens of millions of years.
Leafcutter ants of Central and South America do not eat the leaves they carry.
They chew them into a pulp to feed a fungus in underground gardens, and the fungus becomes their food.
Their nests can hold millions of ants.
Other ants are herders.
They protect aphids and scale insects from predators and collect honeydew, the sugary liquid these insects excrete.
If you see ants running over a plant covered in scale insects, that is this partnership in action.
Some ants even carry their insect 'livestock' to fresh plants to feed.
Australian ant marvels.
In the arid centre, honeypot ant workers called repletes are fed so much nectar and honeydew that their abdomens swell into amber balls the size of a small grape.
They hang from the ceilings of underground chambers as living food stores for lean times.
Aboriginal people have long dug them up as a sweet food.
In the tropical north, green tree ants, also called weaver ants, build nests by pulling leaves together.
Some workers hold the leaves in place while others carry larvae, whose silk glues the leaves together.
Green tree ants are also a traditional bush food, and many people describe their taste as sharp and lemony.
Stings and invaders.
Most ants are harmless, but bull ants and jack jumpers deserve respect.
Their sting is painful.
For a minority who are allergic, especially to jack jumper venom, it can cause life-threatening anaphylaxis.
Jack jumper allergy is well known in Tasmania.
This is general information, not medical advice: difficulty breathing, facial or throat swelling, or collapse need urgent help, so call 000.
People with known allergies should follow their doctor's plan.
Invasive ants are among the world's most damaging pests.
Red imported fire ants were found in Brisbane in 2001 and have been the target of eradication ever since.
On Christmas Island, yellow crazy ants formed supercolonies and killed millions of red crabs.
If you suspect fire ants, report them to the national fire ant program or your state biosecurity agency.
The key idea: Ants are astonishingly abundant, with about 20 quadrillion alive, weighing more than all wild birds and mammals combined.
Part three. Elephants: memory, matriarchs and the meaning of death.
Elephants live in families led by wise old females, talk in rumbles too low for us to hear, and pay strange attention to their dead.
Three species, big lives.
Genetic studies show Africa holds two elephant species, not one.
The savanna elephant is the largest land animal alive, with big males up to about four metres at the shoulder and six tonnes or more.
The forest elephant is smaller, with straighter, downward-pointing tusks, and lives in central and west African rainforest.
The IUCN began assessing them separately in 2021.
The Asian elephant, with smaller ears and a domed head, is a different branch again, more closely related to the extinct woolly mammoth than to either African species.
Elephants eat well over a hundred kilograms a day and can live into their sixties.
They dig waterholes, open thick bush and, in forests, spread seeds in their dung.
Led by grandmothers.
Elephant society is built around females.
A family of related mothers, daughters, sisters and young is led by an older matriarch.
Young males leave in their early to mid teens.
Pregnancy lasts around 22 months, the longest of any land mammal, and the calf, about a hundred kilograms at birth, is helped by aunts and older sisters.
Research in Kenya's Amboseli National Park showed why the matriarch matters.
Families led by older females were better at telling familiar calls from strangers' and reacted most strongly to the most dangerous lion roars.
Older matriarchs also remember routes to water in drought.
When poaching kills them, a lifetime of knowledge is lost.
Talking through the ground.
Elephants trumpet, but much of their conversation is quieter to our ears.
They use deep rumbles, part of which are infrasound, frequencies too low for humans to hear.
These sounds travel far, helping scattered groups keep in touch and males find females ready to mate.
Researchers have also found evidence that elephants detect vibrations travelling through the ground.
Their feet and trunks are packed with sensitive nerve endings, and elephants sometimes freeze, lean forward and press a foot down as if listening.
The trunk is a marvel too: a boneless organ of muscle that can pluck a single blade of grass, suck up litres of water or lift a heavy log, with an extraordinary sense of smell.
Minds and mourning.
Elephants are among the few animals that seem to recognise themselves in a mirror.
In a study published in 2006, an Asian elephant named Happy at the Bronx Zoo repeatedly touched a painted mark on her head that she could see only in her reflection.
Elephants also cooperate on tasks, swat flies with branches and remember individuals for years.
They treat their dead unusually too.
They touch bodies, stand quietly beside them and return over several days.
In Amboseli, elephants showed far more interest in elephant skulls and ivory than in other skulls or wood.
Whether this is grief is still debated.
The old story of elephant graveyards is a myth, though bones can gather near water where weak animals linger.
Evolution by poaching.
Humans have shaped elephants too.
Ivory poaching targets animals with tusks.

In Mozambique's Gorongosa National Park, heavy poaching during the civil war from 1977 to 1992 left a population with a far higher share of tuskless females, because tuskless animals were more likely to survive and breed.
Genetic research published in 2021 confirmed this was evolution driven by hunting.
It is a sobering reminder of how quickly human pressure can change a species, and of the knowledge lost whenever older elephants are killed.
The key idea: There are three living elephant species: African savanna, African forest and Asian elephants.
Part four. Senses beyond our own.
Bats see with sound, turtles read the Earth's magnetism and sharks feel your heartbeat's electricity.
Every animal lives in a different sensory world.
Each animal's own world.
In the early 1900s, the German biologist Jakob von Uexküll used the word umwelt, meaning 'surrounding world', for the slice of reality each animal can sense.
A tick responds to warmth and the smell of butyric acid in mammal sweat; a bee lives in a world of ultraviolet patterns; a dog in a world of scent trails.
Our own umwelt is narrow.
We can't hear the ultrasonic calls of bats, see ultraviolet light or feel electric fields.
Understanding other animals' senses helps explain their behaviour, and has inspired technologies from sonar to medical ultrasound.
It is also a reminder that our view of reality is just one of many.
Sound and scent.
Insect-hunting bats make rapid, mostly ultrasonic calls and listen to the echoes, judging the distance, size, direction and texture of objects well enough to snatch insects in total darkness.
Dolphins echolocate with clicks, and some blind people learn to navigate with tongue clicks.
Australia's large flying foxes mostly don't echolocate; they use good eyesight and smell.
A dog's nose is another marvel: an estimated 200 to 300 million scent receptors, against roughly five or six million in humans, with much of the brain devoted to smell.
Sniffed air goes to a special smelling region, and exhaled air leaves through side slits so it doesn't blow away incoming scent.
Dogs smell far better than we do, by some estimates thousands of times better for certain odours.
Biosecurity detector dogs sniff out undeclared food and plants at airports.
Magnetic and electric.
Many animals detect Earth's magnetic field to navigate, including migratory birds, sea turtles, salmon and some insects.
Caged European robins oriented in their migratory direction, and changed it when the field was altered.
Young sea turtles appear to learn their home coastline's magnetic signature and use it years later to return to nest.
How they sense it is debated: light-sensitive cryptochrome proteins in birds' eyes, tiny iron particles, or both.
Sharks and rays have jelly-filled pores on their snouts, the ampullae of Lorenzini, that detect extremely weak electric fields, such as those from the muscles and heartbeat of a fish buried in sand.
A hammerhead's wide head spreads these sensors to sweep the seabed.
Popular claims that sharks smell one drop of blood from kilometres away are exaggerated.
Colour beyond ours.
Our lens blocks most ultraviolet light, but bees, butterflies, many birds, fish and reptiles see it.
To a bee, flowers that look plain to us carry bold UV patterns called nectar guides that point to pollen and nectar.
Many birds have four types of colour receptor rather than our three.
Reindeer see some UV, which may help them spot lichen and predators against Arctic snow.
Mantis shrimp are often said to see unimaginable rainbows, with up to 16 photoreceptor types, around 12 for colour.
But a 2014 study led by University of Queensland researchers found they are worse than humans at telling similar colours apart.
They may recognise colours quickly and directly, like a barcode scanner.
They can also see circularly polarised light, which is extremely rare.
Myths and lessons.
Goldfish don't have three-second memories; they can learn and remember tasks for months.
Bulls don't charge at red; they are colour-blind to red and react to the movement of the matador's cape.
Other senses are real but under-appreciated: pythons and pit vipers detect body heat with infrared-sensing pits, and many birds hear infrasound far below our range.
The practical lesson: when an animal's behaviour seems strange, ask what it might be sensing.
Your dog may be reading a scent story, and a bird may be seeing colours on a flower that you can't.
The key idea: Each animal senses only a slice of reality, its umwelt, and ours is just one of many.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did gibbons once seem worse than chimpanzees at using tools?
Answer. The test didn't suit their hook-like hands.
Question two. According to a 2022 estimate, how do ants compare with wild birds and mammals by weight?
Answer. Ants outweigh wild birds and mammals combined.
Question three. Why are elephants now generally counted as three species rather than two?
Answer. Genetic studies show two distinct African species.
Question four. What does the word 'umwelt' describe?
Answer. The world as an animal senses it.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
